draft.title: How the spheres interact
card: The atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere are not separate. Energy and matter move between them all the time.
Water is one example. It evaporates from the oceans into the air, falls as rain onto land, and soaks into soil that plants use.
Because the spheres are linked, a change in one can lead to changes in the others. A volcanic eruption throws ash and gases into the atmosphere, and lava and rock add new material to the lithosphere.
The ash can block some sunlight and cool the air for a time. It can also fall on water and soil, and damage plants and animals in the biosphere.
draft.remember: The spheres are linked, so a change in one can bring changes in the others.

a.q: Why can a volcanic eruption affect all four spheres?
opts: Energy and matter move between the spheres
Each sphere reacts to events in its own way
Volcanoes only release material into the lithosphere
The spheres take turns responding to a change
a.why: Ash, gases, water and living things move between the spheres, so a change in one reaches the others. It is wrong to treat each sphere as separate, because the card shows they are linked and do not act alone.
a.clue: Think about what moves between the spheres.

b.q: Heavy rain in a river catchment in northern NSW washes soil from cleared hillsides into a river. Which describes the interaction?
opts: Atmosphere and lithosphere affect the hydrosphere
Hydrosphere changes the atmosphere with no other effect
Lithosphere changes only the biosphere and nothing else
Biosphere moves matter into the atmosphere and stops
b.why: Rain from the atmosphere moves soil, which is part of the lithosphere, into river water in the hydrosphere. The tempting wrong options show a change stopping in one sphere, but the card says changes can lead to changes in others.
b.clue: Name where the rain, the soil and the river each belong.

a.best: Energy and matter move between the spheres

b.best: Atmosphere and lithosphere affect the hydrosphere

problems.detail: The right option is the only one without an absolute limit. Every distractor says 'only', 'nothing else', 'with no other effect' or 'and stops', so a student can reject them without knowing the idea.
The distractor 'Volcanoes only release material into the lithosphere' uses 'only' and contradicts the card's own example of ash and gases entering the atmosphere, so it is too easy to rule out.

The card puts the cooling down to ash blocking sunlight. Ash falls out of the air within days to weeks and can only cool an area locally. The wider cooling 'for a time' after big eruptions comes mainly from sulfur dioxide forming sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere. The card should mention the gases, not just the ash, to avoid teaching a misconception.

check.summary: Both intended answers are correct, but in question b the right option is the only one without an absolute like 'only' or 'stops', which gives it away. The card also credits ash, rather than sulfur gases (sulfate aerosols), with the cooling after eruptions.

proposal.title: How the spheres interact
card: The atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere are not separate. Energy and matter move between them all the time.
Water evaporates from the oceans into the air and falls as rain on land. Running water can then carry soil, which is part of the lithosphere, into rivers.
Because the spheres are linked, a change in one can lead to changes in the others. A volcanic eruption starts in the lithosphere and sends ash and gases into the atmosphere.

Sulfur gases from a large eruption can form tiny droplets high in the atmosphere. These reflect sunlight and can cool the Earth for a time. Falling ash can coat water and soil and harm plants and animals.
proposal.remember: The spheres are linked, so a change in one can bring changes in the others.

a.q: Why can a volcanic eruption affect all four spheres?
opts: Energy and matter move between the spheres
Each sphere is a separate system that reacts alone
The lithosphere controls what happens in the others
A volcano is part of all four spheres at once
a.why: Gases, ash and water move from the eruption into the air, water, soil and living things, so a change in one sphere reaches the others. Treating each sphere as separate misses the point that they are linked.
a.clue: Think about what moves out of the volcano and where it goes.

b.q: Strong winds lift dry soil from paddocks in western NSW and carry it as a dust storm. Which way is matter moving?
opts: From the lithosphere into the atmosphere
From the atmosphere into the lithosphere
From the hydrosphere into the atmosphere
From the biosphere into the lithosphere
b.why: Soil is part of the lithosphere, and the wind carries it up into the air, which is the atmosphere. The reverse is tempting because wind belongs to the atmosphere, but the soil starts on the ground and moves up.
b.clue: Ask where the soil starts and where it ends up.

a.best: Energy and matter move between the spheres

b.best: From the lithosphere into the atmosphere
